The DEBIT (descriptive binary) test

Source: R/debit.R
debit.Rd

debit() checks whether the reported mean and standard deviation of binary data are consistent with the reported sample size. With k ones among n values, the mean is k / n and the SD follows from k and n; the test asks whether any k produces both reported numbers at their decimal places.

The function is vectorized, but debit_map() is more convenient for testing many cases.

Usage

debit(
  x,
  sd,
  n,
  digits_x,
  digits_sd,
  data_type,
  sd_meaning = c("sd_sample", "sd_pop", "sd_sample_or_pop", "se"),
  formula = c("exact", "mean_n"),
  rounding = "up_or_down",
  threshold = 5,
  symmetric = FALSE
)

Arguments

x

Numeric. The reported mean of the binary data, between 0 and 1.

sd

Numeric. The reported standard deviation, between 0 and 1.

n

Integer. The reported sample size.

digits_x, digits_sd

Integer. The number of decimal places in x and sd, including trailing zeros. There are no defaults, since a numeric value does not keep them (1.40 is 1.4).

data_type

String. As in grim(): "integer" or "continuous". No default. For DEBIT, "integer" means the binary values 0 and 1 that the test assumes. Continuous data can have any mean and SD from 0 to 1, so the result is TRUE, but a single value can only have an SD of 0. Values outside of 0 to 1 are an error for either data type.

sd_meaning

String. What sd really is: the sample SD, "sd_sample" (the default); the population SD, "sd_pop"; either one, "sd_sample_or_pop"; or the standard error of the mean, "se". As in grimmer(), whose sections Defaults and SD meaning say why the sample SD is the default and when to choose another.

formula

String. "exact" (the default) only considers means that n binary values can have, i.e., k / n for a whole number k. "mean_n" treats the mean as continuous, as in Heathers and Brown (2019), and accepts some SDs that no binary sample of size n can have: debit(0.05, 0.21, 20, 2, 2, "integer", formula = "mean_n") is TRUE, although a mean of 0.05 with n = 20 means one 1 in 20, whose SD rounds to 0.22.

rounding

String. The rounding method assumed to have produced x and sd. Default is "up_or_down". See grim() for the others.

threshold, symmetric

The same as in grim().

Value

Logical. TRUE if x, sd, and n are consistent, FALSE if not, and NA if the case cannot be decided: if n is not a positive whole number, or if a missing value could decide the case either way. See vignette("technical-notes"), section Missing values, on which cases a missing value leaves open. A sample SD divides by n - 1, so under sd_meaning = "sd_sample" (the default) and "se", n must also be at least 2.

Details

x, sd, n, digits_x, digits_sd, and data_type are vectorized and recycled to a common length by the tidyverse rules. All other arguments must have length 1.

x and sd are limited to about 15 significant digits, and x with n as in grim(). Within these limits, debit() decides value sets of any size exactly. With x missing, n must be below 2^52, about 4.5e15.

References

Heathers, James A. J., and Brown, Nicholas J. L. 2019. DEBIT: A Simple Consistency Test For Binary Data. https://osf.io/5vb3u/.

See also

debit_explain() to explain a result in plain words, debit_map() for data frames, and debit_values() and debit_plot_line() for the means and SDs behind a value set.

Examples

debit(
  x = 0.36,
  sd = 0.11,
  n = 20,
  digits_x = 2,
  digits_sd = 2,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> [1] FALSE
